paper_sections.title: Reduced Functional Connectivity within the Mesocorticolimbic System in Substance Use Disorders: An fMRI Study of Puerto Rican Young Adults

description.value: The study examined whether young adults with substance use disorders showed altered resting-state functional connectivity within the mesocorticolimbic system relative to young adults without substance use disorders, and explored site, impulsivity, and path-analysis relationships.

spans.text: To test our hypothesis that relative to SUD− individuals, SUD+ individuals would have altered functional connectivity within the MCLS, we entered the seed-based connectivity maps into second-level, random-effects general linear models (GLM) with Group as the single factor with two levels (SUD+ and SUD−), and comorbid disorders as a covariate (dummy coded 1 or 0).
We examined associations between a self-report measure of impulsivity (Barratt Impulsiveness Scale, BIS-11(Barratt, 1994 )) and MCLS connectivity.

design.value: A cross-sectional, two-site resting-state fMRI study comparing participants with and without substance use disorders, followed by moderator, correlation, and path analyses.

spans.text: For resting-state image acquisition, participants were instructed to remain still with their eyes closed and to let their minds wander freely.
Participants across the two sites were group-matched on age, sex, and presence of SUD and comorbid psychiatric disorders (Table 1 ).
To test whether the relationship between SUD and altered MCLS connectivity differed at the two sites, we conducted a moderator analysis.

model_settings.value: Two linear regression models followed by bias corrected bootstrapping to test the indirect effect of impulsivity on SUD as mediated by MCLS connectivity.

spans.text: In the first linear regression model, we found that impulsivity was significantly associated with low MCLS connectivity (left NAcc − left OFC connection strength; beta = −0.006, t = −2.13, p = 0.043).
